origin.description: Integrates a first-order ODE system with classical Runge-Kutta of order 4. The step is the difference of successive times.
origin.usage: rk4(y, times, func, parms, verbose = FALSE, ynames = TRUE, dllname = NULL, initfunc = dllname, initpar = parms, rpar = NULL, ipar = NULL, nout = 0, outnames = NULL, forcings = NULL, initforc = NULL, fcontrol = NULL, ...)

arguments.name: y
arguments.text: Initial state. Names label the output columns.

arguments.name: times
arguments.text: Output times. The first value is the initial time.

arguments.name: func
arguments.text: func(t, y, parms, ...) returns a list. The first element is the derivatives, in the same order as y. Later elements are global outputs.

arguments.name: verbose
arguments.text: When TRUE, prints the return code, the step count, the evaluation count, and the order.

arguments.name: ynames
arguments.text: When TRUE, the state passed to func keeps the names of y.

origin.details: The solver takes one fixed step from each time to the next. It does not interpolate, and it does not handle events, roots, or a Jacobian. hmin and hmax warn. hini is printed and ignored. Global outputs are read on a second pass over the stored rows. The logistic series below is the rk4 series from the help example, printed instead of the figure that also draws euler and lsoda.
origin.value: A matrix of class deSolve. Columns are time, the states, and the global outputs. type is rk.

translation.example:
from deSolve.rk4 import rk4

def logist(t, x, parms):
    r = parms["r"]
    K = parms["K"]
    dx = r * x[0] * (1.0 - x[0] / K)
    return [dx]

out = rk4({"N": 0.1}, list(range(0, 101, 2)), logist, {"r": 0.5, "K": 100})
print(out)
